subject: Python
goal: Use Python for machine learning: load and clean data, train models with scikit-learn, and understand what the code does.
scope: This map takes a learner from no Python to training and evaluating scikit-learn models on their own data. It follows the order most Python-for-data-science courses use and the scientific Python stack itself is built on: core Python first, then NumPy, then pandas and plotting, then machine learning with scikit-learn. Core Python is covered in full because reading library code, error messages and documentation needs it. That includes a short topic on classes, because scikit-learn's estimators are objects with methods and fitted attributes. NumPy and pandas cover loading, cleaning, reshaping and exploring data. The machine learning part follows scikit-learn's own organisation: the estimator API, preprocessing and pipelines, supervised models, evaluation, model selection, ensembles and a little unsupervised learning, with concepts like overfitting and data leakage taught where the code needs them. Left out: deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow), the mathematical derivations behind the algorithms, web development, async, concurrency, packaging and publishing libraries, type hints and testing frameworks, and big-data tools. These are worth learning later but are not needed for the stated goal. Seaborn and other plotting libraries are left out in favour of matplotlib and pandas plotting, which are enough for exploring data.

profile.name: Python
profile.trap: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a) prints [1, 2, 3], even though the code never touched a. Assignment in Python never copies anything. It makes a name refer to an object, so a and b are two names for the same list, and changing the list through one name shows through the other. The same rule explains why a function can change a list you pass to it, and why a pandas DataFrame or NumPy slice you 'copied' with = changes the original.
profile.slips: Forgetting the colon after an if or for line, typing pirnt instead of print, a missing closing parenthesis, writing from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegresion, or misspelling a column name like df['prcie'].
profile.observe: Run the code and print things: type(x) and id(x) show what an object is and whether two names share it, a is b tests sameness, and help(obj) or dir(obj) lists what it can do. For data, print df.shape, df.dtypes, df.head() and df.isna().sum() after every step. For models, print the fitted attributes such as model.coef_ or model.classes_. The key habit is to change one thing, run it again and compare the output.
profile.rich: You are given a small DataFrame of houses with a price column, a size column that has some missing values and a text column for the neighbourhood. Split the data into training and test sets, build a pipeline that fills the missing sizes and one-hot encodes the neighbourhood, fit a linear regression, and print the test-set mean absolute error. Then explain why the imputer has to sit inside the pipeline and not be applied before the split.
profile.examples: Short, complete programs that run on their own, each followed by its exact output. Data is built in the code as a tiny list, array or DataFrame, never read from an outside file, and random_state is fixed so a model's printed numbers are the same on every run.

nodes.name: Running code: scripts, the REPL and notebooks
nodes.what: Run Python code three ways: as a saved script from the command line, line by line in the REPL, and cell by cell in a notebook. You will know when each one is the right choice.

nodes.name: print() and comments
nodes.what: Use print() to show values on screen and write comments with # to explain code. You can then see what a program is doing and leave notes for yourself.

nodes.name: Variables as names for values
nodes.what: Understand that a variable is a name pointing at a value, not a box holding it. You can assign, reassign and choose good names.

nodes.name: Numbers: int, float and arithmetic
nodes.what: Work with ints and floats and use the arithmetic operators, including // and %, ** and operator precedence. You can predict what an expression evaluates to.

nodes.name: Floating-point rounding surprises
nodes.what: Understand why 0.1 + 0.2 does not equal 0.3 exactly, because floats are stored in binary. You will compare floats safely with a tolerance and round for display.

nodes.name: Strings and string methods
nodes.what: Create strings and use common methods such as upper, strip, split, join, replace and find. You know that strings are immutable and can be indexed.

nodes.name: f-strings for formatting output
nodes.what: Build readable output with f-strings, embedding expressions and format specifiers such as {x:.2f}. You can print tidy tables and messages with values in them.

nodes.name: Booleans, comparisons and None
nodes.what: Use True and False, the comparison operators (==, !=, <, >=) and the None value that means 'no value'. You can tell == from is and know what a comparison returns.

nodes.name: Converting between types
nodes.what: Convert values with int(), float(), str() and bool(), and know when a conversion fails. You can turn user or file text into numbers before computing with it.

nodes.name: if, elif and else
nodes.what: Make code take different paths with if, elif and else. You can write branching logic and understand how indentation marks each block.

nodes.name: and, or, not and truthiness
nodes.what: Combine conditions with and, or and not, and know which values count as false (0, empty collections, None). You can write short conditions such as 'if items:' and understand short-circuit evaluation.

nodes.name: for loops and range()
nodes.what: Repeat work with for loops over a range or over the items of a sequence. You can control the start, stop and step of range() and loop a fixed number of times.

nodes.name: while loops
nodes.what: Repeat code while a condition holds, using a while loop. You can avoid infinite loops by updating the condition and know when while is better than for.

nodes.name: break and continue
nodes.what: Leave a loop early with break or skip to the next iteration with continue. You can use them to stop a search once you have found a result or to skip unwanted items.

nodes.name: Looping with enumerate() and zip()
nodes.what: Use enumerate() to get an index with each item and zip() to walk several sequences in step. This replaces manual index counters and is common when pairing features with labels.

nodes.name: Lists: creating, indexing and appending
nodes.what: Create lists, read items by index (including negative indexes) and add items with append and extend. You know that lists are ordered and can change.

nodes.name: Slicing sequences
nodes.what: Take parts of a list or string with [start:stop:step], including negative indexes and the reverse slice [::-1]. You can predict which items a slice includes and excludes.

nodes.name: Tuples and unpacking
nodes.what: Use tuples as fixed groups of values and unpack them into several names in one assignment. You can swap values and return multiple values neatly.

nodes.name: Dictionaries: keys, values and lookup
nodes.what: Store and look up values by key in a dictionary, with d[key], get(), adding and deleting entries, and the `in` test for keys. You can model records as key-value pairs.

nodes.name: Looping over dictionaries
nodes.what: Loop over a dictionary's keys, values or key-value pairs with keys(), values() and items(). You can pick the right view for the job.

nodes.name: Sets
nodes.what: Use sets for unique items, fast membership tests and set operations such as union, intersection and difference. You can remove duplicates from a list.

nodes.name: List and dictionary comprehensions
nodes.what: Build lists and dictionaries in one line with comprehensions, including an optional if filter. You can read and write them in place of simple loops that append.

nodes.name: Mutability: aliasing and copying
nodes.what: Understand that two names can point to the same mutable object, so changing one changes the other. You will know how to make a shallow or deep copy when you need an independent one.

nodes.name: Defining and calling functions
nodes.what: Define a function with def, give it parameters and call it with arguments. You can wrap repeated steps into a reusable, named block.

nodes.name: Return values
nodes.what: Send results back from a function with return, including returning several values as a tuple. You know that a function without return gives None.

nodes.name: Default and keyword arguments
nodes.what: Give parameters default values and call functions with keyword arguments. You can read calls such as f(x, n=3), which scikit-learn uses everywhere.

nodes.name: *args and **kwargs
nodes.what: Accept any number of positional arguments with *args and keyword arguments with **kwargs, and unpack a list or dict into a call with * and **. You can read function signatures that use them.

nodes.name: Local and global scope
nodes.what: Know which names a function can see: local names, global names and the order Python searches for them. You will understand why assigning inside a function does not change a global and when the global keyword applies.

nodes.name: Mutable default arguments
nodes.what: Recognise the bug that comes from using a mutable value such as [] as a default argument, because it is created once and shared between calls. You can use None as the default instead.

nodes.name: Lambda functions
nodes.what: Write small anonymous functions with lambda and pass them as arguments, for example as a key= for sorting. You can read lambdas in other people's code.

nodes.name: Docstrings and help()
nodes.what: Document a function with a docstring and read documentation with help() or ?. You can find out what any function does and what arguments it takes.

nodes.name: Reading a traceback
nodes.what: Read a traceback from the bottom up: the exception type and message first, then the line and chain of calls that led to it. You can find where the error came from.

nodes.name: Common exceptions: TypeError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError
nodes.what: Recognise what causes TypeError, KeyError, IndexError and ValueError, and the usual fix for each. You can diagnose most beginner errors from the message alone.

nodes.name: try and except
nodes.what: Catch errors with try, except, else and finally and handle specific exception types. You can keep a program running when an expected failure happens, without hiding real bugs.

nodes.name: Raising exceptions
nodes.what: Signal a problem yourself with raise and a clear message, for example when a function gets a bad argument. You can choose a suitable built-in exception type.

nodes.name: Debugging with print() and assert
nodes.what: Find bugs by printing intermediate values and checking assumptions with assert. You will learn a simple routine for narrowing down where a program goes wrong.

nodes.name: import and from ... import
nodes.what: Bring code from another module into your program with import, import ... as and from ... import, and know how each form changes the names you can use. Recognise how Python finds the module and why you write math.sqrt but sqrt after a from-import.

nodes.name: Useful standard library modules: math, random, collections
nodes.what: Use a handful of standard library modules for everyday jobs: math for functions like sqrt and pi, random for random choices and numbers, and collections for tools like Counter and defaultdict. Look up other modules in the library reference when you need them.

nodes.name: Installing packages with pip
nodes.what: Install third-party packages such as numpy, pandas and scikit-learn with pip install, check what is installed with pip list, and pin versions. Understand that pip downloads packages from PyPI into the Python you are running.

nodes.name: Virtual environments
nodes.what: Create and activate a virtual environment so each project has its own packages and versions. Explain why this avoids version conflicts and how to recreate an environment from a requirements file.

nodes.name: Writing your own module
nodes.what: Put functions in your own .py file and import them from another script or notebook. Understand the role of the if __name__ == '__main__' guard and where Python looks for your module.

nodes.name: Reading and writing text files with open() and with
nodes.what: Open a text file with open() inside a with block, read it whole or line by line, and write or append to it. Explain why with closes the file for you and how modes ('r', 'w', 'a') and encoding matter.

nodes.name: File paths with pathlib
nodes.what: Build and inspect file paths with pathlib.Path: join parts with /, check whether a path exists, list files with glob, and read a file's name or suffix. Write paths that work on any operating system instead of gluing strings together.

nodes.name: Reading CSV and JSON with the standard library
nodes.what: Read and write CSV files with the csv module and JSON files with the json module, turning rows and objects into lists and dictionaries and back. Understand how this differs from pandas, which you will use later for the same job.

nodes.name: Objects, attributes and methods
nodes.what: See that every value in Python is an object with attributes (data) and methods (functions that belong to it), reached with dot notation. Use methods on strings, lists and other built-in objects and tell an attribute from a method call.

nodes.name: Defining a class with __init__ and self
nodes.what: Write a class with an __init__ method that sets attributes on self, add methods, and create instances from it. Understand what self refers to and that each instance keeps its own data, as in scikit-learn estimators.

nodes.name: Inheritance and overriding methods
nodes.what: Create a subclass that inherits attributes and methods from a parent class, override a method, and call the parent's version with super(). Understand why scikit-learn models are built as classes that inherit shared behaviour.

nodes.name: Special methods: __repr__, __len__ and friends
nodes.what: Define special (dunder) methods such as __repr__, __str__, __len__ and __getitem__ so your objects work with print(), len() and indexing. Understand that built-in functions and operators call these methods behind the scenes.

nodes.name: Duck typing: objects that share an interface
nodes.what: Explain duck typing: code works with any object that has the methods it needs, whatever its class. Recognise this in practice, such as any estimator with fit and predict being usable in the same code.

nodes.name: Iterables and iterators
nodes.what: Distinguish an iterable (something you can loop over) from an iterator (something that hands out values one at a time with next()). Explain what a for loop does with them and why an iterator can be used up once.

nodes.name: Generators and yield
nodes.what: Write a generator function with yield that produces values one at a time without building a whole list, and use generator expressions. Understand how this saves memory when working through large data.

nodes.name: Creating arrays
nodes.what: Create NumPy arrays from lists with np.array, and with np.zeros, np.ones, np.arange and np.linspace. Explain how an array differs from a Python list.

nodes.name: dtype and shape
nodes.what: Read an array's dtype, shape, ndim and size, and explain what they mean for 1-D, 2-D and higher arrays. Choose or change a dtype with astype and see how it affects memory and results.

nodes.name: Indexing and slicing arrays
nodes.what: Pick out elements, rows, columns and sub-blocks of an array with index and slice notation such as a[1, 2] and a[:, 0]. Extend what you know about list slicing to several dimensions.

nodes.name: Views versus copies in NumPy
nodes.what: Know that a basic slice of an array is a view that shares memory with the original, while fancy indexing, boolean masks and .copy() make copies. Predict when changing one array changes another and use .copy() to avoid surprises.

nodes.name: Boolean masks
nodes.what: Build a boolean array from a comparison like a > 0 and use it to select matching elements or assign to them. Combine conditions with & and | and count matches with sum.

nodes.name: Fancy indexing with integer arrays
nodes.what: Select or reorder array elements by passing a list or array of integer positions, for example a[[0, 2, 5]]. Understand that the result is a copy and how this differs from slicing.

nodes.name: Vectorized arithmetic and ufuncs
nodes.what: Do arithmetic on whole arrays at once with +, *, ** and ufuncs such as np.sqrt, np.exp and np.log, with no explicit loop. Explain why this is faster and shorter than looping over a list.

nodes.name: Aggregations along an axis
nodes.what: Compute sum, mean, min, max and std over a whole array or along an axis, for example one value per column or per row. Say which axis to choose and what shape the result has.

nodes.name: Broadcasting
nodes.what: Predict how NumPy combines arrays of different shapes, such as subtracting a column mean from every row, by applying the broadcasting rules. Spot when shapes are incompatible and fix them.

nodes.name: Reshaping, stacking and transposing
nodes.what: Change an array's shape with reshape (including -1), flatten or ravel, transpose with .T, and join arrays with np.concatenate, np.vstack and np.hstack. Use newaxis or reshape to turn a 1-D array into a column.

nodes.name: Matrix multiplication with @
nodes.what: Multiply matrices and compute dot products with the @ operator and np.dot, and check that the shapes line up. Tell it apart from element-wise * and see how it underlies linear models.

nodes.name: NaN and infinity in arrays
nodes.what: Recognise np.nan and np.inf, see how they spread through calculations, and detect them with np.isnan and np.isinf. Use nan-aware functions like np.nanmean and understand that nan != nan.

nodes.name: Random numbers and seeds
nodes.what: Generate random numbers and samples with NumPy's random generator (np.random.default_rng), and set a seed so results repeat. Explain why seeding matters for reproducible experiments.

nodes.name: Series and DataFrame
nodes.what: Explain what a Series (one labeled column of values) and a DataFrame (a table of Series sharing an index) are, and build small ones from lists and dictionaries.

nodes.name: The index
nodes.what: Understand that every Series and DataFrame carries an index of row labels, and how to set, reset and use it so that labels (not just positions) identify rows.

nodes.name: Loading data with read_csv
nodes.what: Load a CSV file into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv and use its common options such as sep, header, index_col, usecols and dtype.

nodes.name: Inspecting data: head, info, describe
nodes.what: Get a quick first look at a dataset with head, tail, shape, info and describe, and read from the output the column types, non-null counts and basic statistics.

nodes.name: Selecting columns
nodes.what: Select one column with df['col'] or several with df[['a', 'b']], and know when you get back a Series and when a DataFrame.

nodes.name: Selecting rows with loc and iloc
nodes.what: Select rows and columns by label with loc and by integer position with iloc, and explain how slices differ between the two.

nodes.name: Filtering rows with conditions
nodes.what: Keep only the rows that meet one or more conditions using boolean expressions, combining them with & and | and brackets.

nodes.name: Adding and transforming columns
nodes.what: Create new columns and transform existing ones from other columns with vectorized arithmetic and simple column methods such as map and replace.

nodes.name: Chained assignment and Copy-on-Write
nodes.what: Recognize why chained indexing like df[df.x > 0]['y'] = 1 does not change the original DataFrame: since pandas 3.0, Copy-on-Write is the default, so every indexing result behaves as a copy and chained assignment never writes back (older versions sometimes did and showed SettingWithCopyWarning instead). Assign safely in one step with df.loc[rows, col] = value, or work on an explicit .copy().

nodes.name: Finding missing values
nodes.what: Find missing values (NaN/None) with isna and notna, and count them per column and per row to see how much of a dataset is incomplete.

nodes.name: Dropping and filling missing values in pandas
nodes.what: Handle missing data in pandas by dropping rows or columns with dropna and by filling with fillna (a constant, the mean, or neighbouring values), and judge which choice suits a given column.

nodes.name: Fixing column types with astype and to_numeric
nodes.what: Convert columns to the right type with astype and pd.to_numeric (including errors='coerce' for messy strings) so that numeric work and models treat them correctly.

nodes.name: Removing duplicates
nodes.what: Detect duplicate rows with duplicated, remove them with drop_duplicates, and choose which columns define a duplicate and which copy to keep.

nodes.name: Cleaning text columns with .str
nodes.what: Clean text columns in bulk using the .str accessor: strip whitespace, change case, replace and extract patterns, and split strings.

nodes.name: Parsing dates with to_datetime
nodes.what: Turn date and time strings into real datetime values with pd.to_datetime, handle formats and unparseable entries, and pull out parts such as year or weekday with .dt.

nodes.name: Categorical columns and value_counts
nodes.what: Inspect and tidy categorical columns with value_counts and unique, spot inconsistent labels or rare categories, and use the category dtype.

nodes.name: Spotting outliers
nodes.what: Spot unusual values using summary statistics, the IQR rule and z-scores, and decide whether an outlier is an error to fix or a real value to keep.

nodes.name: Sorting rows
nodes.what: Order a DataFrame by one or more columns or by its index with sort_values and sort_index, in ascending or descending order.

nodes.name: groupby and aggregation
nodes.what: Split data into groups with groupby, compute summaries such as mean, count or several statistics per group with agg, and read the result.

nodes.name: Merging DataFrames
nodes.what: Combine two DataFrames side by side on shared keys with merge or join, and explain inner, left, right and outer joins and what happens to unmatched rows.

nodes.name: Concatenating DataFrames
nodes.what: Stack DataFrames on top of each other (or side by side) with pd.concat, and handle mismatched columns and the resulting index.

nodes.name: Pivot tables and melt
nodes.what: Reshape tables between wide and long form with pivot_table and melt, and summarize one measure across two categories.

nodes.name: apply and when to avoid it
nodes.what: Use apply to run your own function over the rows or columns of a DataFrame, and explain why built-in vectorized operations are usually faster and clearer.

nodes.name: Line and scatter plots with matplotlib
nodes.what: Draw line plots and scatter plots with matplotlib and add titles, axis labels, legends and colours so a plot can be read by someone else.

nodes.name: Figures, axes and subplots
nodes.what: Explain the Figure and Axes objects, create several plots in one figure with plt.subplots, and draw on a chosen Axes.

nodes.name: Histograms and box plots
nodes.what: Show how a numeric variable is distributed with histograms and compare groups or find outliers with box plots, and read both.

nodes.name: Plotting directly from pandas
nodes.what: Make quick plots straight from a Series or DataFrame with the .plot methods (line, bar, hist, scatter, box) and pass them an Axes.

nodes.name: Correlation matrices and heatmaps
nodes.what: Compute a correlation matrix with df.corr, draw it as a heatmap, and interpret what correlation does and does not say, including its link to features and target.

nodes.name: What a model learns: features, target and parameters
nodes.what: Describe a model as a function that maps input features to a target, whose parameters are fitted from example data rather than written by hand.

nodes.name: Supervised versus unsupervised learning
nodes.what: Tell supervised learning (examples come with known targets) from unsupervised learning (finding structure with no target) and classify a problem as one or the other.

nodes.name: Regression versus classification
nodes.what: Decide whether a problem is regression (predict a number) or classification (predict a category) and name typical examples of each.

nodes.name: Training and test sets
nodes.what: Explain why data is split into a training set to fit the model and a test set to estimate how it performs on new data, and why testing on the training data misleads.

nodes.name: Overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance tradeoff
nodes.what: Recognize overfitting (memorizing the training data) and underfitting (too simple), connect them to model complexity and the bias-variance tradeoff, and tell them apart by comparing training and test scores.

nodes.name: Data leakage
nodes.what: Understand data leakage, where information from the test set or the future gets into training, give common examples such as scaling before splitting, and see why it inflates scores.

nodes.name: The feature matrix X and target y
nodes.what: Arrange data as a 2-D feature matrix X (rows are samples, columns are features) and a 1-D target y, and check their shapes before handing them to scikit-learn.

nodes.name: Estimators: fit and predict
nodes.what: Use the estimator pattern: create a model object, call fit(X, y) to learn from data, then predict(X_new) to get predictions.

nodes.name: Transformers: fit, transform and fit_transform
nodes.what: Explain how transformers learn something from data in fit, apply it in transform, and combine both with fit_transform, and why the fitted values are reused on new data.

nodes.name: Splitting data with train_test_split
nodes.what: Split X and y into training and test portions with train_test_split, and control the test size and shuffling.

nodes.name: Hyperparameters versus fitted attributes (the trailing underscore)
nodes.what: Tell apart hyperparameters, which you set when creating the model, from fitted attributes ending in an underscore, which are learned by fit, and look at both with get_params and the attributes.

nodes.name: random_state and reproducibility
nodes.what: Set random_state so splits and randomized models give the same results on every run, and know why results can differ without it.

nodes.name: Scaling features: StandardScaler and MinMaxScaler
nodes.what: Rescale numeric features with StandardScaler or MinMaxScaler, fitting only on training data, and explain why distance-based and regularized models need it.

nodes.name: Encoding categories with OneHotEncoder
nodes.what: Turn categorical columns into 0/1 indicator columns with OneHotEncoder, and handle categories that appear only in new data.

nodes.name: Imputing missing values in a model with SimpleImputer
nodes.what: Fill missing values inside a model workflow with SimpleImputer so the fill values are learned from training data only.

nodes.name: ColumnTransformer for mixed column types
nodes.what: Apply different transformers to different columns (for example scale numbers and one-hot encode categories) with ColumnTransformer and get one combined feature matrix.

nodes.name: Pipelines
nodes.what: Chain preprocessing steps and a final model into a single Pipeline that is fitted and used like one estimator, and see how this prevents leakage.

nodes.name: Polynomial and interaction features
nodes.what: Create squared and interaction features with PolynomialFeatures so a linear model can fit curved relationships, and recognise the risk of too many features.

nodes.name: Linear regression
nodes.what: Fit a linear regression model with LinearRegression and understand that it finds the straight line or plane that minimizes squared error.

nodes.name: Reading coefficients and the intercept
nodes.what: Read coef_ and intercept_ to say how the prediction changes when a feature goes up by one unit, and know why scale affects how comparable coefficients are.

nodes.name: Regularization: Ridge and Lasso
nodes.what: Use Ridge and Lasso to penalize large coefficients, see how the alpha hyperparameter trades fit against simplicity, and know that Lasso can set coefficients to exactly zero.

nodes.name: Regression metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE and R²
nodes.what: Compute MAE, MSE, RMSE and R² on predictions, explain what each one measures, and choose among them for a problem.

nodes.name: Logistic regression
nodes.what: Fit LogisticRegression for classification and explain that it models class probabilities from a weighted sum of features, with C controlling regularization.

nodes.name: k-nearest neighbors
nodes.what: Classify a point by the majority class among its k closest training points, and see how k and feature scaling change the result.

nodes.name: Decision trees
nodes.what: Fit a DecisionTreeClassifier, read the splits it makes, and use max_depth and similar settings to control overfitting.

nodes.name: Support vector machines
nodes.what: Use a support vector classifier to find a wide-margin boundary, and understand the roles of the kernel and C.

nodes.name: predict_proba and decision thresholds
nodes.what: Get class probabilities with predict_proba and turn them into labels with a chosen threshold instead of the default 0.5.

nodes.name: Baselines with DummyClassifier
nodes.what: Build a baseline with DummyClassifier (for example always predicting the most common class) and use it as the score a real model must beat.

nodes.name: Accuracy and its limits on imbalanced data
nodes.what: Compute accuracy and explain why it can look high while being useless when one class is much rarer than the other.

nodes.name: Confusion matrix
nodes.what: Read a confusion matrix to count true and false positives and negatives and see which kinds of mistakes a classifier makes.

nodes.name: Precision, recall and F1
nodes.what: Compute precision, recall and F1 from the confusion matrix, and pick which one matters for a given cost of mistakes.

nodes.name: ROC curve and AUC
nodes.what: Read an ROC curve and AUC as a summary of how well a classifier ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds.

nodes.name: Cross-validation with cross_val_score
nodes.what: Estimate model performance more reliably by splitting the training data into folds and averaging scores with cross_val_score.

nodes.name: Choosing a splitter: KFold, StratifiedKFold and GroupKFold
nodes.what: Pick a cross-validation splitter that suits the data: KFold in general, StratifiedKFold for imbalanced classes, GroupKFold when rows from one group must stay together.

nodes.name: Grid search with GridSearchCV
nodes.what: Search a grid of hyperparameter values with GridSearchCV, using cross-validation, and read best_params_ and best_score_.

nodes.name: Randomized search with RandomizedSearchCV
nodes.what: Sample hyperparameter combinations at random from distributions with RandomizedSearchCV to cover large search spaces at a fixed budget.

nodes.name: Learning curves and validation curves
nodes.what: Plot learning curves and validation curves to tell whether a model suffers from high bias or high variance and whether more data or a different setting would help.

nodes.name: Keeping a final test set untouched
nodes.what: Set aside a final test set that is used once, after all tuning, and explain why repeated peeking at it makes the score too optimistic.

nodes.name: Random forests
nodes.what: Train a RandomForest, which averages many decorrelated trees built on random samples and features, and understand why this reduces overfitting compared with a single tree.

nodes.name: Gradient boosting with HistGradientBoosting
nodes.what: Use HistGradientBoostingClassifier or Regressor, which builds trees one after another to correct earlier errors, and tune its main settings such as learning rate and number of iterations.

nodes.name: Feature importances and permutation importance
nodes.what: Rank features by impurity-based importances and by permutation importance on held-out data, and know when each one can mislead.

nodes.name: k-means clustering
nodes.what: Understand how k-means groups unlabeled rows by repeatedly assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving the centroids, and fit KMeans in scikit-learn to get cluster labels and centers. Know that you must choose the number of clusters yourself and that results depend on the starting centroids.

nodes.name: Choosing the number of clusters: inertia and silhouette
nodes.what: Use inertia (the elbow plot) and the silhouette score to compare different values of k, and explain why neither gives a single certain answer. Be able to judge whether a clustering is sensible rather than just accepting the output.

nodes.name: PCA for dimensionality reduction
nodes.what: Use PCA to project many numeric features onto a few new directions that keep most of the variance, and read explained_variance_ratio_ to decide how many components to keep. Understand why features should usually be scaled first and that the components are mixtures of the original columns.

nodes.name: An end-to-end ML workflow from CSV to evaluated model
nodes.what: Carry out a whole project: load a CSV with pandas, split off a test set, build a preprocessing and model pipeline, tune it with cross-validation, and report an honest score on untouched test data. Be able to explain what each stage does and why it comes in that order.

nodes.name: Saving and loading models with joblib
nodes.what: Save a fitted model or whole pipeline to a file with joblib.dump and load it again with joblib.load to make predictions without retraining. Know that the file is tied to the library versions used and should only be loaded if you trust its source.

nodes.name: Reading the scikit-learn documentation
nodes.what: Navigate the scikit-learn documentation: find an estimator's API page, read its parameters, attributes and examples, and use the user guide to learn an unfamiliar model. Be able to work out for yourself what a parameter does and how to use a class you have not met.

why.t1: The learner needs to run code in scripts and notebooks and use print() to see what the code is doing.
why.t2: Formatted output with f-strings and converting text to numbers are everyday steps when working with data and model results.
why.t3: Branching and loops, including enumerate and zip for pairing features with labels, are needed to read and write ML code.
why.t4: Tuple unpacking (as in train_test_split), comprehensions and an understanding of aliasing and copying are needed to follow typical ML code.
why.t5: Return values, keyword arguments, *args/**kwargs and docstrings are how scikit-learn functions are called and documented.
why.t6: Reading tracebacks and common exceptions and debugging with print and assert are essential for fixing code that fails on real data.
why.t7: The learner must install pandas and scikit-learn with pip and keep project packages apart in virtual environments.
why.t9: scikit-learn models are objects of classes with shared interfaces, so understanding objects, classes, inheritance and duck typing explains what the code does.
why.t11: Feature matrices are NumPy arrays, so indexing, slicing and boolean masks are needed to work with them.
why.t12: Aggregation, broadcasting, reshaping, matrix multiplication, NaN handling and seeds underlie scaling, linear models and reproducible experiments.
why.t13: Loading, inspecting, selecting, filtering and transforming columns with pandas is the core of loading data, and chained assignment is a common cleaning pitfall.
why.t14: Cleaning data is a named part of the goal: missing values, types, duplicates, text, dates, categories and outliers.
why.t15: Grouping and aggregating gives summaries by category that help in understanding a dataset before modelling.
why.t16: Distributions, quick pandas plots and correlation heatmaps are how data is explored before training models.
why.t17: The learner needs the core ideas of features, targets, train and test sets, overfitting and leakage to train models sensibly.
why.t18: The estimator and transformer API, X and y, splitting, hyperparameters and random_state are how every scikit-learn model is used.
why.t19: Scaling, encoding, imputing, column transformers and pipelines prepare cleaned data for models without leakage.
why.t20: Regression models, their coefficients, regularization and metrics are a main use of scikit-learn.
why.t21: Logistic regression, nearest neighbors, trees and probabilities are the standard classification models to train.
why.t22: Training a classifier is only useful if it can be evaluated honestly, with baselines, confusion matrices, precision and recall, and AUC.
why.t23: Cross-validation, hyperparameter search, learning curves and a final test set are how models are tuned and scored reliably.
why.t24: Random forests and gradient boosting are strong, widely used scikit-learn models, and importances help explain them.
why.t26: An end-to-end project and reading the scikit-learn documentation tie everything together and let the learner continue on their own.

route.note: No current level was given, so I picked the points the goal itself uses (pandas loading and cleaning, the scikit-learn workflow, evaluation) plus the Python and NumPy ideas needed to read ML code, and left prerequisites to the page. I left out files with the standard library, generators, string-only details, PCA and clustering, and other topics the goal does not use.

fixes.text: Renamed "Chained assignment and SettingWithCopyWarning" to "Chained assignment and Copy-on-Write" (Since pandas 3.0, Copy-on-Write is the default and SettingWithCopyWarning has been removed. Chained assignment now always fails to update the original, so 'can fail' and the warning describe the old behaviour.)
"Pipelines" now needs "Data leakage" first (The point says pipelines prevent leakage, and that makes no sense without first knowing what data leakage is.)

"An end-to-end ML workflow from CSV to evaluated model" now needs "Grid search with GridSearchCV" first (The end-to-end project tunes the pipeline with cross-validation, which is the grid search taught in p127. p125 alone only scores a model and does not tune it.)

"Splitting data with train_test_split" now needs "Tuples and unpacking" first (train_test_split returns four arrays that are unpacked in one assignment (X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = ...), so it relies on tuple unpacking.)

"Learning curves and validation curves" now needs "Line and scatter plots with matplotlib" first (The point asks the learner to plot learning and validation curves, which needs basic matplotlib plotting.)

"k-nearest neighbors" now needs "Scaling features: StandardScaler and MinMaxScaler" first (Seeing how feature scaling changes k-nearest neighbors needs the scalers, and the reason distance-based models need them, taught in p105.)
"Accuracy and its limits on imbalanced data" now needs "Estimators: fit and predict" first (Computing accuracy compares a model's predictions with the true labels, so it needs fit and predict first.)

"Series and DataFrame" now needs "import and from ... import" first (Building a Series or DataFrame starts with import pandas as pd. Every other library entry point on the map (p52, p67, p88) needs p37, and this one should too.)

checks.verdict: The map is sound. Its scope, order and route fit the goal well. The fixes update one point that described pandas behaviour from before Copy-on-Write became the default, and fill in a few missing prerequisite links, mainly in the machine-learning topics.
